name: emio
workload: emio::scan with compile-time or runtime format strings (nothing, simple int, 64-bit int, hex) versus sscanf, run with Catch2 BENCHMARK in test/benchmark/bench_scan.cpp.
claimed_speedup: "Scanning on the other hand is around twice as fast then scanf." (docs/DESIGN.md, Performance section). Formatting is stated to be "round about 1.5 - 2 times slower than fmtlib" and "similar to printf (e.g. for integer types)".
tradeoffs: Targets bare-metal and RTOS embedded systems: no exceptions (returns emio::result), works without heap, about 5 kBytes versus 191 kBytes of flash for fmt on a one-line format (38 times smaller, per DESIGN.md). Supports fewer features than fmt. C++20 required (GCC 11-13, Clang 16-17 tested). Library is labelled beta.
caveats: Single prose sentence of numbers in DESIGN.md; no result table, compiler, flags or CPU are stated, and no benchmark output is committed (the Catch2 benchmarks run inside CI). The sscanf baseline is the C library, so the C library vendor is unknown. Its own formatting numbers say it is slower than fmt (1.5-2x) and about equal to printf, so the speed win is scanning only; the headline win is binary size, not speed.

name: ExprTk
baseline: muParser 2.2.4 (also FParser 4.5, TinyExpr, ATMSP, METL, MathExpr, MTParser, Lepton, muparserx)
workload: Evaluate pre-parsed expressions (parse once, evaluate many times) with variables a, b, c, x, y, z, w; each of 74 expressions in bench_expr.txt evaluated 5,000,000 times, ranked per expression, points summed.
claimed_speedup: README example summary: ExprTk (double) 901 points, score 100; muparser 2.2.4 517 points, score 37; FParser 4.5 584 points, score 43; TinyExpr 354 points, score 31; atmsp 530 points, score 38. Per-expression example: ExprTk 39.963 ns versus muparser 2.2.4 47.358 ns on '(a^2/sin(2*pi/b))-a/2'. Score 100 versus 37 is about 2.7x (derived from page data; the README says only that the reference parser is ExprTk).
compiler_and_flags: MSVC 1913 (Visual Studio 2017), Release|Win32 (32-bit): /O2 MaxSpeed, InlineFunctionExpansion AnySuitable, FavorSizeOrSpeed Speed, /fp:precise, NDEBUG, _SECURE_SCL=0 per the repo's msvc2017 vcxproj (flags are not printed in the results log); the repo .pro file builds with g++ -std=c++11 -march=native -fopenmp
hardware: Intel Xeon E5-2687W 0 @ 3.10GHz, 8 cores / 16 logical, L3 20480 KB
tradeoffs: Header-only (very large single header, long compile times), runtime parse into an expression tree with optional constant folding; supports scalars, vectors, strings, loops and user functions. Heavy template use hits compile time and binary size.
caveats: The shootout suite is maintained by ExprTk's own author, so it is first-party even though code, compiler and CPU are public. The README summary is labelled an example; the committed 2018 log logs/shootout_20180421_00.zip (bench_expr_complete.txt, 6617 expressions, 100000 iterations, same Xeon and MSVC 1913) shows ExprTk 77945 points score 100 versus muparser 2.2.4 51672 points score 28, FParser 4.5 score 32, TinyExpr score 15 (I read that log from a downloaded zip, not from the README page). muparserSSE (float, 78987 points, score 167) beat ExprTk (double) in that log, and ExprTkFloat scored 86. Several rival parsers are old versions bundled in the repo ('may contain outdated versions'), and the benchmark is 32-bit MSVC only. Last-commit date is the year-stamped commit date from the GitHub commit feed (2025-01-01 is how the author dates commits).

name: FANN (Fast Artificial Neural Network Library)
baseline: Lightweight Neural Network (lwnn 0.6) and Jet's Neural Library (jneural 1.05)
workload: Execution time per connection (nanoseconds) for running fully connected ANNs with 128 neurons per layer on an AMD Athlon XP 1600+ (1400 MHz) and on a 206 MHz StrongARM iPAQ H3600 without an FPU, from Steffen Nissen's 2003 FANN report.
claimed_speedup: AMD Athlon, 128 neurons per layer: "fann (thres) library is 238.583 times faster than the jneural library and the fann library is 164.388 times faster than the jneural library"; lwnn at 127.074 times jneural (4.007 ns per connection versus jneural 509.138), so fann is about 1.3x lwnn (derived from page data). iPAQ: fann (fix) 188.134 ns per connection, about 70 times faster than jneural and 2.7 times faster than jneural on the Athlon workstation. README: "up to 150 times faster execution than other libraries".
compiler_and_flags: Same compiler and compile options for all three libraries per the report; compiler and flags not named on the page
hardware: AMD Athlon XP 1600+ (1400 MHz, 256 KB L2) and 206 MHz Intel StrongARM iPAQ H3600, both Linux
stars_or_usage: 1.8k stars; packaged in Debian, Fedora and vcpkg
tradeoffs: Multilayer perceptrons only (RPROP, Quickprop, batch, incremental, Cascade2), CPU only, no GPU or convolutions; fixed-point mode exists for FPU-less devices; cache-optimised layout. LGPL.
caveats: Author's own 2003 report, measured on 2003 hardware against two obscure libraries (jneural, lwnn); no comparison with any current ML library. The benchmark code is not in the current repo (no benchmarks directory). The WebFetch summaries of the report page disagreed on the per-library ns values between reads (for example fann at 3.1 or 3.3 ns), so only the sentences and ratios that repeated across reads are quoted here: 238.583x, 164.388x, 127.074x, the 2.7x iPAQ remark. At 512 neurons per layer, fann and lwnn timings were reported as equal in one read. The README '150 times' figure names no baseline.

name: FastFormat
baseline: C stdio snprintf (printf family), plus C++ IOStreams and Boost.Format
workload: Seven formatting scenarios (statement forms not spelled out on the results page), average time relative to FastFormat.Format, over Ubuntu x86/x64 and Windows x86/x64 with GCC 4.1, GCC 4.2, Visual C++ 6 and Visual C++ 9; FastFormat 0.2.1 beta 6.
claimed_speedup: Time of snprintf relative to FastFormat.Format (above 1.0 means FastFormat faster), scenarios 1-7: 1.49, 0.83, 1.15, 0.66, 1.63, 6.87, 1.64 (so faster in 5 of 7, slower in scenarios 2 and 4). IOStreams 3.28, 2.16, 5.08, 2.41, 2.82, 9.96, 2.86. Boost.Format 10.29, 5.18, 12.10, 5.57, 8.68, 17.27, 8.94. FastFormat.Write 0.74, 0.84, 0.61, 0.81, 0.70, 0.88, 0.71. Page headline: 5 - 17 times faster than Boost.Format, 1.5 - 5.5 times faster than Loki.SafeFormat.
compiler_and_flags: GCC 4.1, GCC 4.2, Visual C++ 6, Visual C++ 9; optimisation flags not stated
tradeoffs: Type-safe, no format-string parsing for the Write API; relies on the STLSoft and Pantheios-style support libraries and sink objects; Format (replacement-based, I18N friendly) is slower than Write (concatenation-based). Needs its own inserter functions for user types.
caveats: Author's own page from 2008-2009 era toolchains (VC6, GCC 4.1/4.2); no CPU, RAM, flags or date on the page, and the scenario definitions sit on sub-pages that were not opened. snprintf beat FastFormat.Format in scenarios 2 and 4 (0.83 and 0.66), so the printf win depends on scenario and compiler. Averages mix platforms and compilers. The repo's FAQ says 'make test.performance' reproduces the claims; the repo now carries a boilerplate/CMake revival (last commit titled 'Boilerplate (#4)'). The ACCU Overload 91 article by the author could not be opened (egress blocked); a web search snippet reports 3x faster than C streams, 6x faster than IOStreams, 17x faster than Boost.Format in a realistic scenario with Visual C++ 9 on 32-bit Windows.

name: FastNoiseSIMD
workload: Time to generate 32x32x32 points of 3D noise on a single thread, default noise settings, for white, value, Perlin, simplex, cellular and cubic noise; libnoise has Perlin and cellular rows only.
claimed_speedup: Times in x1000 ns. Perlin: AVX512 147, AVX2 324, SSE4.1 592, SSE2 795 versus FastNoise 1002 and LibNoise 1368. Cellular: AVX512 851, AVX2 1283, SSE4.1 2679, SSE2 2959 versus FastNoise 2979 and LibNoise 58125. Simplex: AVX512 129, AVX2 294 versus FastNoise 1194. Cubic SSE2 3516 versus FastNoise 2979 (slower). Versus LibNoise (derived from page data): Perlin 9.3x (AVX512), 4.2x (AVX2), 1.7x (SSE2); cellular 68x (AVX512), 45x (AVX2), 20x (SSE2). README text: 'increasing performance by 700% in some cases (Simplex)'.
hardware: Intel Xeon Skylake @ 2.0 GHz, single thread
tradeoffs: Runtime detection of the best instruction set (AVX-512F, AVX2 with FMA3, SSE4.1, SSE2, ARM NEON) with a scalar fallback; 3D noise sets only; noise values differ from the scalar FastNoise implementation; the author deprecated it in favour of FastNoise 2.
caveats: First-party table from an ICC-built binary on one Skylake Xeon; the benchmark program is a separate preview app in Releases and its code and the libnoise version are not stated. The cellular row against libnoise (68x) is above 50x and likely reflects libnoise's cellular implementation rather than SIMD alone. The scalar FastNoise baseline is the same author's library, and cubic SSE2 is slower than it. Repository archived 2 April 2021 and marked deprecated; AVX-512 numbers need a Skylake-X class CPU.
